decks.domain: Search, speed, space and signaling confusables

cards.front: How does the manual say driving skills are gained?
cards.back: Driving skills come only through practice and experience, and the manual offers these tips as things to practice to become a safer, more skillful driver.

cards.front: What must you know before starting and while driving?
cards.back: Before starting the vehicle and while driving, you must know what is happening around you by looking ahead, to the sides and behind.

cards.front: What eye habit should you develop for every drive?
cards.back: Develop a searching pattern for your eyes and use it every time you drive.

cards.front: Why should you keep your eyes moving instead of staring?
cards.back: Searching shows you situations that could become a problem and gives you time to change your speed or road position, so keep your eyes moving instead of staring at any one thing.

cards.front: What does looking well down your planned path give you?
cards.back: Looking well down your planned path gives you time to adjust and plan, leads to better decisions and may spare you from emergency braking and steering.

cards.front: How far ahead should you ideally watch?
cards.back: Ideally, try to watch what is happening twenty to thirty seconds ahead of your vehicle.

cards.front: How can you keep from limiting how far you can see?
cards.back: Avoid situations that cut how far you can see, such as following a larger vehicle too closely, and adjust your speed and road position to see best.

cards.front: How does your sight distance in a city compare with a highway?
cards.back: How far ahead you can look depends on where you drive, and in cities and urban areas you may not see as far as on a highway.

cards.front: Why should you search to the sides of your vehicle?
cards.back: Search to the sides of your vehicle to see whether other road users are about to cross your path.

cards.front: When is it especially important to check traffic behind you?
cards.back: Stay aware of traffic behind you, using your mirrors, especially when you change lanes, slow down or stop, or enter an intersection.

decks.module: Speed for curves and wet roads
decks.domain: Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating

cards.front: What does driving at a safe speed involve?
cards.back: Driving safely means adjusting your speed to road and traffic conditions, keeping an adequate following distance and obeying the speed limits that apply.

cards.front: When should you slow down for a curve, and to what speed?
cards.back: Always slow down before you enter a curve, to a safe speed that lets you apply slight and constant acceleration all the way through it.

cards.front: When should you slow even more for a curve?
cards.back: Slow down even more on a curve when traction is poor, when you are following other vehicles and when you cannot see where the curve ends.

cards.front: Why should you brake before a curve rather than in it?
cards.back: Speed should come down before the curve, because hard braking after you have entered it could make the tires lose traction.

cards.front: When should you reduce speed in bad weather?
cards.back: Reduce your speed at the first sign of rain, snow, sleet or ice.

cards.front: How does a slippery road affect stopping and turning?
cards.back: On a slippery road your tires grip less, so stopping takes longer and turning without skidding is harder.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning?
cards.back: Hydroplaning is when your steering tires end up riding on a film of water above the road surface, much like water skis.

cards.front: What is the best way to avoid hydroplaning?
cards.back: The best way to avoid losing traction to hydroplaning is to slow down in the rain or on roads with pooled water or puddles.

cards.front: What should you do if a road ahead is flooded or barricaded?
cards.back: If you see a flooded road, or barricades blocking one, find another route to where you are going.

cards.front: How quickly can flash floods arrive?
cards.back: Flash floods can come quickly and without warning, within a few minutes or hours of excessive rainfall.

cards.front: What can cause flooding on roads?
cards.back: Flooding can come from rivers and streams overflowing, dams or levees breaking, run-off from deep snow or any heavy rainfall, and floodwater gathers on roads, bridges and low areas.

cards.front: Why take special care around possible flooding at night?
cards.back: Take special care at night around possible flooding, when visibility is limited.

cards.front: What can six inches of water do to most passenger cars?
cards.back: Six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling.

cards.front: What can two feet of moving water do?
cards.back: Two feet of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks.

cards.front: How do the six-inch and two-foot water depths differ in danger?
cards.back: Six inches of water is enough to reach the underside of most passenger cars, while two feet of moving water can carry away even SUVs and pickups.
cards.memory_hook: Stall at six, float at two

cards.front: Why should you never cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow?
cards.back: Never try to cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow, because the water can hide dips and other hazards and can wash away the road's underlying surface.

cards.front: What should you do if there is no other route around floodwater?
cards.back: If no other route exists, drive to higher ground and wait for the floodwater to go down.

decks.domain: Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating

cards.front: What is total stopping distance?
cards.back: Total stopping distance is how far your vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the moment you realize you must stop until it actually stops.

cards.front: How does speed affect stopping?
cards.back: The faster you are going, the more time and distance you need to stop.

cards.front: What is perception time, and how long does it average?
cards.back: Perception time is the time and distance it takes to recognize that you must stop, and for an alert driver it averages ¾ second to one second.

cards.front: What is reaction time, and how long does it average?
cards.back: Reaction time is the time and distance it takes to move your foot from the gas pedal and start braking, and it averages ¾ second to one second.

cards.front: How do perception time and reaction time differ?
cards.back: Perception time is about recognizing that you must stop, while reaction time is about moving your foot from the gas to the brake, and both average ¾ second to one second.

cards.front: What is braking distance, and how far does it take at highway speed?
cards.back: Braking distance is the time and distance your brakes need to stop the vehicle, about one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes.

decks.domain: Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating

cards.front: What is a space cushion, and why keep one?
cards.back: The more space you leave between you and other road users, the more time you have to react; this space is called a space cushion, and you should keep one all around your vehicle.

cards.front: What happens when you follow the vehicle ahead too closely?
cards.back: Following the vehicle ahead too closely limits your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision.

cards.front: What minimum following distance should you keep?
cards.back: Always try to keep a following distance of at least four seconds behind the vehicle in front.

cards.front: How do you count your following distance?
cards.back: To check the gap, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or other fixed point, then count one thousand one, one thousand two and so on until you reach that point.

cards.front: What do you do if you reach the fixed point before counting to four?
cards.back: If you reach the fixed point before counting to one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and count again at another point until the gap is at least four seconds.

cards.front: How can you practice judging the four-second gap?
cards.back: You can test how well you judge the four-second gap by guessing how many seconds away an object is and then counting the seconds it takes to reach it.

cards.front: When should you increase following distance on the road surface?
cards.back: Increase your following distance on slippery roads.

cards.front: When else should you leave extra following room?
cards.back: Also leave more room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings such as transit buses, school buses and hazardous materials carriers, and behind large vehicles like trucks, buses, RVs and vehicles towing trailers.

decks.domain: Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating

cards.front: Why should you avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches?
cards.back: Avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches, because you may sit in their blind spot and lose the side space you might need to avoid a crash.
cards.memory_hook: Do not ride in blind spots

cards.front: How should you position yourself relative to the centerline?
cards.back: Do not crowd the centerline, and keep as much room as you can between you and oncoming traffic.

cards.front: How can you help vehicles joining a multi-lane road?
cards.back: Make room for vehicles joining a multi-lane or limited access road by moving over a lane or adjusting your speed.

cards.front: Who deserves extra space on the road?
cards.back: Give pedestrians extra space, especially children, elderly people and bicyclists.

cards.front: What should you do when a tractor trailer passes you?
cards.back: When a tractor trailer passes you, give it more room by moving to the outer part of your lane, away from the truck.

cards.front: How can you help the driver behind you keep a safe distance?
cards.back: You can help the driver behind you keep a safe distance by holding a steady speed, signaling early and leaving extra room ahead before you slow down or turn.

decks.domain: Safe driving tips: visual search, speed management, stopping distance, space management and communicating

cards.front: When do headlights especially help others see you?
cards.back: Headlights help others see you, especially on rainy, snowy or foggy days, when you should use low beams and slow down, and as it gets dark or when you drive away from a rising or setting sun.

cards.front: Which lights should you use on rainy, snowy or foggy days?
cards.back: On rainy, snowy or foggy days the manual says to drive with your low-beam lights on and to slow down.

cards.front: When is a light horn tap useful?
cards.back: A light horn tap is useful when pedestrians or bicyclists seem to be moving into your lane, when you pass a driver who starts turning into your lane, or when a driver is not paying attention or may not see you.

cards.front: How much horn is normally enough?
cards.back: Under normal circumstances a light tap on the horn should be all you need.

cards.front: When should you use the horn, and when not?
cards.back: Use the horn only to communicate, since misuse can scare or anger other road users, and do not use it near blind pedestrians.

cards.front: Should you use the horn near blind pedestrians?
cards.back: The horn is a tool for getting attention when needed, but near blind pedestrians it should not be used at all.

cards.front: How far ahead does South Carolina law require a turn signal?
cards.back: South Carolina law requires a turn signal at least one hundred feet before you change lanes, turn left or right, or merge into traffic.

cards.front: What should you do with your signal after a lane change or turn?
cards.back: Once a lane change, turn or merge is finished, cancel your signal so other drivers are not confused.

cards.front: When should you signal before slowing down?
cards.back: Brake lights tell others you are slowing, and you should signal before slowing when turning off a road that has no separate turn or exit lane, or when parking or turning just before an intersection.

cards.front: Are brake lights enough when you slow to leave a road with no turn lane?
cards.back: Brake lights show you are slowing, but you should also signal before slowing when you leave a road that has no separate turn or exit lane.

recap_hooks.text: Keep your eyes moving in a searching pattern, look twenty to thirty seconds ahead, and check the mirrors before changing speed or lanes.

recaps.module: Speed for curves and wet roads

recap_hooks.text: Slow down before curves and at the first sign of rain, and slow in wet weather to avoid hydroplaning.
Never drive into floodwater: six inches can stall a car and two feet of moving water can sweep it away.
Stopping takes perception time, reaction time and braking distance, and every bit of it grows with speed.
Keep at least four seconds behind the car ahead, counting from a fixed point, and add more in poor conditions.
Do not linger beside other vehicles, stay off the centerline and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room.
Signal at least one hundred feet before you move, use low beams in bad weather, and use the horn only to communicate.
